doc.title: Dawoud Sabu Adeyola interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, January 30, 2025

title: First paid bass gig, Local 533 and union merger
summary: Elvin Shepherd paid him first; story of segregated Local 533, its merger with Local 43, and Perry Gray keeping the building.

story.theme_name: The musicians' union: cards, locals, and the Black-white merger
story.community_name: The musicians' union: cards, scale and the black-white merger

blocks.x: Do you remember the first time you got paid to play your bass?
Yes, yes. I do. It was from a man named Elvin Shepherd. You know about Elvin Shepherd?
I see his name on your promo material.

Elvin Shepherd was a great musician. He was Grover Washington’s teacher. And when Grover went, if you ever see any interviews about Grover Washington and they ask him about, like you asked me about my background, he always goes on and on and on about how great Elvin Shepherd was. And Elvin Shepherd was a member of the Local 533, the black musicians union, which is a whole ‘nother story. I was so blessed to be a part of that. I joined that union six months before it was dissolved. You know? I mean the union, the white union and the black union were merged by mandate. It was mandated. The merger — there were about almost 20 cities and Buffalo that had segregated unions. And in 1953 they started merging, and Los Angeles was the first one. Benny Carter was a big part of that. Benny Carter, because of his stature, I mean he’s the king you know, and he got involved with the union. I mean you had to be in the union but being in L.A. with all the entertainment movies and stuff and he led, he said, even then he was saying man it’s crazy, why should we have two unions? I mean the black union and the white? This is crazy. So he led the move to integrate the unions out there and ’53 and ’54 that was the first one. Gradually they all started merging, especially after the Civil Rights Act of ’65, which said that segregation is illegal. Buffalo was the very last one to do it. You know?
Did you notice a positive or negative circumstances that followed that merging of the union?

I saw both actually. I mean in the long run it was good because segregation in any form, you know based on race, gender, religion, is always — I mean even as a kid I was raised in the African Methodist Episcopal Zion Church and I used to wonder why — I mean it was segregated you know what I mean? If you — if a white person came to serve, to worship and sat down, people would be wondering oh, who is that? What’s he doing here? You know. I mean this was in the ‘50s you know, up north in Buffalo. And so we had this segreg — as Malcolm X said one time, he said, “the most segregated time in America is 12 o’clock on Sundays” you know. So anyway how did I go there? You were asking about the after-effect. In the long run it was positive because you know it broke down this law that was actually — it was sanctions you know, just like segregation and even slavery was sanctioned by the government and by the Constitution and this thing went on into labor unions so in that sense it was good that it was no longer the law of the land, because it was actually illegal. But in terms of the actual impact on the ground, black musicians suffered you know, because even though the union was formed on it because they were refusing to listen to the white union at Local 43 at that time you know. And so it was formed out of necessity because if you wanted to work you had to have a union card. And so one of the guys, you know, one of the white musicians came over and he was against it. He didn’t agree with it. And he sat down with some of these blacks and he said, “Listen you guys, if they won’t let you join you probably should form your own union.” And he knew how to do it, you know? So he helped form Local 533. And he told them you have to form it — at that time there were two kinds of black unions. One was called a subsidiary union, which was under the control and under the supervision of the white union. They had almost no authority. They had a union but to do anything they had to go over there to the office over there and when they had the national conventions they weren’t invited, they couldn’t vote, you know what I mean? But then you had independent autonomous unions which this guys said you’ve got to get that autonomous part. “You guys would be autonomous. You’ve got to vote, you’re a legitimate union just like any other.” So that’s what Local 533 was. But they had developed a lot of things that even 43 didn’t have. They had a credit union, they had death benefits, you know they had I mean a credit union, I mean, that’s a bank. I mean they set this up way back in the ‘20s and ‘30s. They were pretty smart. They had a bank account that was about triple the size of the other one you know. So, and they had a building, all right? Which still, as you know, is there. So we lost everything pretty much in the merger because you know the larger union kind of swallows up the assets of the small one. They lost everything but the
building. And the reason they didn’t lose the building is because it was incorporated away from the union. It has its own incorporation status.
I see. That’s a great story.

And it was a great thing because they said listen this segregation thing is not going to last and when they merge the other union is going to come in and they’re going to swallow up all your assets, including your real estate. And so when it came the president of the old union, they actually came over and asked for the key you know. Yeah. He said, “Well we’ll take the key, we’ll take the building now.” So the president, his name was Perry Gray, he was a shrewd guy you know. He said, “You want the key, okay, I’ll tell you what. Come upstairs I’ll buy you a drink.” So they’re sitting there, “So what are you having?” So he gave him — “Give him what he wants” you know. So he was sitting there drinking and he said, “Now, about this key, look up over the bar there, you see that Certificate of Incorporation? It’s called the Musicians Club Incorporated, it has nothing to do with the union. Sorry sir, no key.”
Enjoy. Right, right. So that’s a story — the old guys love to tell that story. Yeah, man, the guy came over here to ask for the key, can you imagine that?
